16nav8p:234: A widely overlooked issue in enterprise AI transformation: the more polished the frontend AI application, the heavier the backend unstructured data governance debt. Zhang Sensen described this phenomenon with a precise metaphor—"the frontend is very beautiful, the backend is a mess." A case from the automotive industry shows: when leadership demands "AI as fast as possible," the team, given weak data and governance foundations, can only choose the easiest path to visible results (such as AI coding), while real data governance work is deferred, causing technical debt to accumulate. This "showcase project → technical debt accumulation → increased system fragility" pattern is harder to repay than traditional software engineering debt, because it involves large volumes of uncontrollable unstructured data.
172uvac:333: Ma Jinlong (Qiming Zhiyuan), whose team spun off from its parent company, provided a real case of building an AI Native organization from scratch. Three key insights: (1) Information is primarily formatted so AI can understand it—all documents must be in Markdown, PDF/Word strictly prohibited; AI is the main force, humans are the support (a fundamental shift in role perception); (2) Domains that cannot be AI-ified, such as finance and legal, are explicitly handled by humans—no need to force AI Native; (3) Stay open about current judgments—model capabilities 6-18 months from now may overturn today's architectural assumptions. At the practical level: the team no longer differentiates roles between frontend, backend, testing, and algorithms; "one person, empowered by AI, becomes a hexahedron," with AI covering 70-80% of the work and humans handling judgment and checks. The biggest difficulty has paradoxically become "finding the right problems"—"it's not solutions that are scarce now; it's problems, it's pain points."

1eynvkt:263: The historical analogy proposed by Zheng Yan (Huawei) is highly insightful: factories in the steam engine era placed a large steam engine at the center of the plant, driving all machines through main shafts and belts. When electrification arrived, British factories simply replaced the steam engine with an electric motor and left everything else unchanged. The real production revolution—the assembly line—was achieved by Ford in America. This analogy precisely illustrates: merely layering AI technology on top of an old organizational structure ("swapping engines") without redesigning business processes and organizational structure cannot achieve true AI transformation. "If you really want to transform, you may actually need to start from a very small company state"—this explains why AI transformation in large enterprises always "makes much noise but delivers little rain," while startups can more easily achieve an AI Native organizational form.

1hvhv6i:232: Zhang Sensen analyzed two typical pathological motivations for enterprises adopting AI: first, "the business is hitting a bottleneck, and they hope to take an AI pill to cure their disease"; second, "they see other companies taking AI 'miracle pills' and accelerating, so they feel anxious and must take one too." The essence of both motivations is treating AI as a "wish-granting" tool—"I'll just make a wish, and whether it comes true? That's for AI to help achieve." The result is that companies treat AI as a cost-cutting tool (layoffs) rather than an opportunity for process reinvention. "If the process doesn't change, if it isn't an AI Native process, this company's competitiveness will vanish. Every company is engaged in homogeneous competition, doing the same things."
